Urban Amphibian Microbiota | Manuscript in prep

Contrasting fire salamander dermal microbiota within and urban-rural matrix

Marques, A.J.D, Gaun, N., Velo-Antón, G., Alberdi, A.

2025-06-02

Abstract

Introduction

What are the threats toward amphibians? Amphibians are a metaphorical canary in the coal mine when it comes to global biodiversity loss, vulnerable to multiple threats, of which many may co-occur or compound (Luedtke et al. 2023). The leading cause to amphibians’ declines is habitat loss and degradation, primarily through agriculture and urbanization, the latter of which dramatically changes habitat structures and increases the intensity of environmental stressors including changes in hydrology, temperature, and connectivity (Hamer and McDonnell 2008; Scheffers and Paszkowski 2012; Barrett and Price 2014; Yang, Zhao, and Liu 2022). Another leading cause of declines, particularly in Europe, Australia, and the Americas, has been the spread of fungal chytrid pathogens (O’Hanlon et al. 2018; Rollins-Smith and Le Sage 2021), Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd, Longcore, Pessier, and Nichols (1999)) and Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans (Bsal, Martel et al. (2013)), which have resulted in catastrophic mortality events among naive amphibian populations Fisher and Garner (2020). Efforts to model the spread of fungal pathogens have considered environmental conditions (Crawshaw et al. 2022; Thumsová et al. 2025), but the effect of land-use change and urbanization on fungal risk remains largely unknown (D. Saenz, Hall, and Kwiatkowski 2015; Bacigalupe et al. 2017).

Why are we focused on microbiota? In an effort to understand the fungus’ pathology (Van Rooij et al. 2015), studies have examined the role that dermal microbiota have in amphibians’ ability to resist fungal infections (Muletz-Wolz et al. 2017; Le Sage et al. 2021; González-Serrano et al. 2025). Following fungal exposure, studies have examined how microbiota communities respond to infections in an effort to understand the lasting effect and possible resistance among amphibians (Jani et al. 2021; Bletz et al. 2018). While our understanding of the role microbiota play in anti-fungal resistance is still developing, the urgency of the crisis has led some to propose interventions which may include modifying microbiota as a means to reinforce vulnerable populations (Bletz et al. 2013; Rebollar, Martínez-Ugalde, and Orta 2020; Kueneman et al. 2022). While less covered among amphibians, urban soil and water are prone to contamination from industrial and agricultural proximity (Duong and Lee 2011; Cachada et al. 2012), may also impact the microbiota of urban environments and residents (Muletz et al. 2012; Hu et al. 2018; McLellan, Fisher, and Newton 2015). Cities should also not be discounted for their potential benefits, however, as urban green spaces may provide refuges for wildlife species (Clevenot, Carré, and Pech 2018; Schmidt and Garroway 2021; Gentili et al. 2024). Among the few attempts to model chytrid fungal distributions, also suggested significantly lower rates of occurrences among urban habitats (saenz_urbanization_2015?). The precise causal factor remains unknown, however, experimental studies suggest increased temperatures may impede chytrid fungal growth (Robak et al. 2023) and have observed that ephemeral ponds have lower chytrid fungal loads than permanent water bodies (V. Saenz et al. 2025).

What has been done already? To date, the majority of studies that have begun work characterizing amphibian microbiota have done so through targeting sequencing of 16S (Barnes et al. 2021; Santos et al. 2023). Amplicon enrichment metabarcoding utilizes existing microbial databases to identify the taxonomy of prokaryotes in a manner that is generally accessible and comparable between studies (Pruesse et al. 2007; Quast et al. 2013). Comparative studies using microbial metabarcoding identified significant variations in microbiota assemblage along urbanization gradients, but not necessarily a difference in diversity therein (Jiménez and Sommer 2017; Barnes et al. 2021; Basanta et al. 2022; Zhou et al. 2023). While suitable for repeatable taxonomic identification of prokaryote taxa, amplicon sequencing often yields a coarser taxonomic resolution and does not capture any of the functional variation which may occur within microbiome communities (Campanaro et al. 2018). To improve both the taxonomic and community assemblage resolution, we instead applied a shotgun sequencing method to generate metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs) Ranjan et al. (2016). By assembling short-read sequences into genome assemblies, we can gain improved taxonomic resolution (Ziesemer et al. 2015) and functional gene information (Bates et al. 2022; Eisenhofer, Odriozola, and Alberdi 2023). Additionally, because this methodology uses a very minimal enrichment step, the relative abundance of taxa is better preserved (Gloor et al. 2017). The compromise with this approach, however, is that host DNA is inevitably captured as well and generally comprises the majority of the sequence reads (Pereira-Marques et al. 2019). Removing host DNA generally entails mappings reads to a reference, which in the case of amphibians are often unavailable and difficult to construct owing to the often large size and complexity of amphibian genomes (Sun, López Arriaza, and Mueller 2012; Liedtke et al. 2018). Using a metagenomics approach, we aimed to collect information on how an amphibian species’ microbiome community assemblages may change in composition and function along an urbanization gradient.

What are we hypothesizing? To test this we sampled fire salamanders (Salamandra salamandra; Linnaeus 1758) from within and around the city of Porto, Portugal. Fire salamanders are a widely dispersed and abundant amphibian species typically associated with forest biomes (Wagner et al. 2020; Velo-Antón and Buckley 2015), but can also be found within a variety of urban green spaces (Lourenço et al. 2017; Iglesias-Carrasco, Martín, and Cabido 2017). Fire salamanders are affected by the spread of Bsal (Martel et al. 2013), with microbiome communities that may either resist or exacerbate fungal pathology (Bletz et al. 2018; Smith et al. 2018). To our knowledge Fire salamanders have thus far only ever been subject to 16S amplicon sequencing, and while characterization of the microbiome at variable life stages and habitats are available (Sanchez et al. 2017; Bletz et al. 2018; Afonso et al. 2022), misses out on the more detailed taxonomic and functional resolution that shotgun sequencing provides. Based on comparisons of other amphibian species, we would not necessarily expect a difference in community diversity does not change between communities, instead we hypothesize that compositional shifts in microbiota assemblages will be observed between urban and rural sites. Similarly, we hypothesize that differences in community assemblage will also correspond with functional variation in the microbiota of different habitats.

Methods

Sampling

Porto is a large urban matrix comprised of isolated urban parks of varying size and extensive forested areas comprised of both endemic and invasive tree species. Individuals were collected between mid October to early November of 2023, on nights of high humidity and when temperatures range from 14-22 ºC. This coincides with a season of peak activity, when males move above the leaf litter and present themselves as mating candidates and can be distinguished by the presence of enlarged cloacas. Using sterile gloves, individuals were collect and placed in small individualized sterile containers, ideally avoiding direct contact with salamanders, instead scooping them into the containers to reduce contact with the dermis or contamination between individuals. Salamanders were then moved to laboratory facilities the following morning to proceed with swabbing.

During swabbing a technician wearing sterile gloves (replace between samples) restrained individual salamanders by the base of the tail, using sterile paper towel to help maintain a grip. Individual were then sprayed thoroughly with distilled H2O to remove debris from the dermis. Once rinsed, the individual dermis will be swabbed ten times on the dorsal, ventral, and each side with a swab then placed in a 2 mL tube pre-filled with PBS buffer and frozen at -20ºC. After swabbing individuals are returned to their individual containers then returned to the sampled location later the same day.

Sequencing

Samples were processed in October 2024 at the Globe Institute’s (University of Copenhagen) molecular laboratory in Copenhagen, Denmark, following the established EHI laboratory protocols available at www.earthhologenome.org/laboratory (Pietroni et al. 2025). Samples underwent bead-beating to before DNA isolation employing silica magnetic beads with solid-phase reversible immobilisation. The concentration of DNA extracts was quantified using a Qubit™ 3 Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Subsequently, DNA was fragmented into approximately 450 bp-long fragments using a Covaris LE220 platform. Library preparation followed the ligation-based BEST protocol (Carøe et al. 2018), utilising a standard input of 200 ng of DNA in 24 µl or the closest amount feasible based on the sample DNA concentration. We used 1.5 µl of 20 µM adaptors for a 50-200 ng DNA input, 1.5 µl of 10 µM for 10-50 ng, 1.5 µl of 5 µM for <10 ng, and 1.5 µl of 2 µM for samples below the quantification range of the Qubit® dsDNA HS (High Sensitivity) Assay Kits. Libraries underwent qPCR screening to determine the optimal number of library indexing PCR cycles (Murray, Coghlan, and Bunce 2015), followed by PCR amplification using unique dual index primers with an adjusted number of cycles. The resulting libraries underwent automated capillary electrophoresis (Bioanalyzer or Fragment Analyzer) for assessment of fragment-length distribution, adaptor dimers, and adaptor-to-library molar ratios. Finally, samples were pooled into multiple sequencing batches, and sequencing was performed across multiple lanes of NovaSeq6000 and NovaSeq X platforms (Illumina, USA), generating a ___ GB (approximately ____ million reads) of 150 bp paired-end sequencing data per sample.

Bioinformatics

Raw metagenomic reads were processed following the bioinformatic workflow by the Earth Hologenome Initiative (https://www.earthhologenome.org/; see Leonard et al. (2024)), and stored in the Electronic Research Data Archive (ERDA) of the University of Copenhagen. Computation was conducted in the local cluster of the Globe Institute (Mjolnir) using the snakemake- and slurm-based bioinformatic pipelines tailored to the platform (https://github.com/earthhologenome/EHI_bioinformatics/tree/mjolnir). Quality filtering to remove adapters, low-quality reads (phred >= 20), short reads (>= 60 bp), and polyG/polyX tails was done with Fastp v.0.23.4 (Chen et al. 2018). With skin swabs, the majority of DNA extracted is expected to belong to the host, and so the proportion of prokaryotic sequences were estimated using SingleM microbial fraction (Eisenhofer, Alberdi, and Woodcroft 2024). Host-derived reads were removed by mapping against a reference host genome using Bowtie2 v.2.5.1 (Langmead and Salzberg 2012) and Samtools v.1.18 (Danecek et al. 2021). In the absence of a reference genome for S. salamandra, we used a Salamandra salamandra transcriptome (NCBI RefSeq HBZU010000000; Libro et al. (2023)) in addition to the reference genome of Pleurodeles waltl (NCBI RefSeq assembly GCF_031143425.1; Brown et al. (2025)) which is the next most phylogenetically related species with a reference genome available (Zhang et al. 2008). Unmapped metagenomic reads were assembled into contigs then into putative bacterial genomes known as metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) by MEGAHIT v.1.2.9 (li_2016?). The quality of these MAGs for subsequent downstream analyses was evaluated with Quast (Gurevich et al. 2013) and contig coverage was determined by CoverM (Aroney et al. 2025). Metagenomic binning was performed by multiple algorithms, including CONCOCT v.1.1 (Alneberg et al. 2014), MetaBAT2 v.1.7 (Kang et al. 2019), and MaxBin2 v.2.2.4 (Wu, Simmons, and Singer 2016), the refined by MetaWRAP (Uritskiy, DiRuggiero, and Taylor 2018) into consensus bins. Taxonomical annotations of MAGs were matched to the Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) with the taxonomic classification toolkit (GTDB-Tk) (Chaumeil et al. 2022; Parks et al. 2022). Genome-Inferred Functional Traits (GIFTs) of MAGs were assigned with DRAM (Shaffer et al. 2020) using the Pfam (Finn et al. 2016), KEGG (Kanehisa et al. 2017), UniProt (McGarvey et al. 2019), CAZY (Cantarel et al. 2009), and MEROPS (Rawlings and Barrett 1999) databases and distillR (available at https://github.com/anttonalberdi/distillR). An average nucleotide identity (ANI) of 98% and a minimum genome completeness of 50% were used to dereplicate highly similar MAGs using dRep (Olm et al. 2017). Reads were then mapped to a MAG catalogue to extract quantitative read-abundance information to calculate relative abundance of each MAG per sample, retaining only those with completeness values above 50% and contamination levels below 10% (Bowers et al. 2017).

Statistics

For each sample, we calculated the proportion of sequenced bases that were filtered de to poor quality, unmapped, mapped to the host, and mapped to a MAG. The domain-adjusted mapping rate (DAMR) was used to quantify microbial genome recovery from metagenomes, calculated as the rate of read mapping to sets of microbial genomes (MAGs or other references) divided by the fraction of the community predicted to be prokaryote [Eisenhofer, Alberdi, and Woodcroft (2024). Differences in the proportion of mapped bases between habitats was determined through a Wilcox rank test (Bauer 1972). Additionally, MAG compistion was measured as the relative abundance of each MAG was determined as the number of assigned reads as a proportion of the MAG length divided by average read length to (Gloor and Reid 2016; Gloor et al. 2017), with a Tukey’s Honest Significant Difference test (TukeyHSD, Tukey (1953)) to identify significant differences in relative abundance between habitats at the phylum, class, and family taxonomic scale.

Dissimilarities between site and habitat MAGs composition were calculated in terms of richness as well as neutral, phylogenetic and functional beta diversities using Hill numbers (Hill 1973; Chao, Chiu, and Jost 2014). while considering community richness (q = 0), evenness (q > 0), and disparity between groups. Neutral Hill numbers represent species diversity without considering the degree of relatedness among MAGs; phylogenetic Hill numbers incorporate branch-length information of the phylogenetic tree of the MAGs; functional Hill numbers consider functional differences among MAGs (Hernández et al. 2024) calculated using Hilldiv2 v.2.0.2 (Alberdi and Gilbert 2019). The betadisper function in vegan v.2.6-10 (Oksanen et al. 2013) was applied to test differences in dispersion within sampling methods. PERMANOVA was performed to test for differences in microbial composition between sampling methods using the adonis2 function in vegan, with individual identity as a blocking factor to control for repeated sampling using the strata function. Once again, Wilcoxon rank sum test was used to test for differences in the variance within each group when comparing habitats and an analysis of variance (ANOVA; Chambers and Hastie (1992)) was used to compare differences in variance between sites. To visualize bacteria according to their functional features, the MAGs were ordinated based on their GIFTs through a t-SNE analysis using the Rtsne package v.0.17 (Krijthe and Van der Maaten 2015)

All statistical analyses were performed using the R software v.4.5.0 (R Core Team, 2025).

Taxonomic and Functional Variation

Results

Sequencing libraries included a total of 60 swabs used to generate approximately 105M total reads (mean ± SD = 1.75 ± 2.69, median = 1.11, M reads per sample) of short-read DNA sequencing data. Quality filtering and host read removal resulted in 98.5M filtered reads (mean ± SD = 1.69 ± 2.68 , median = 0.991, Gb per sample) metagenomic data, which were assembled into 119 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) that passed our minimum quality criteria (CheckM2 estimated completeness >50%, contamination <10%). With a mean 4.42 ± 1.89 Gb per sample, on average 5.8% were mapped to MAGs, while 5.3% were removed for low quality, 0.3% mapped to the host, and a substantial 88.6% were unmapped. The domain adjusted mapping rate was that an estimated 22.5 ± 20.8 % of reads were successfully mapped to MAGs.

No significant differences were observed in the filter reads counts between sites or habitats.

The mean proportion of estimated prokaryote reads per sample was 32.92 ± 21.8, however, the mean proportion of reads assigned to MAGs was only 6.37 ± 7.8. Wilcox Test significant lower proportion of bases assigned to MAGs among urban samples as compared to rural samples (W = 709, p = 0.0001).

Taxonomy and Function

Majority of MAGs identified were ascribed to phyla Bacteroidota (33.61%), Pseudomonadota (30.25%), and Bacillota_A (17.65%)

(p)Bacteroidota (f)Chitinophagaceae is observed exclusively among samples from urban habitats, specifically a few individuals from Carrizal.

(p)Actinomycetota (f)Pseudonocardiaceae and (p)Bacillota (f)Erysipelotrichaceae are two Families with several identified taxa observed exclusively among samples from rural habitats. The former is specific to Vairão and the latter is among the most sparsely represented families.

Majority of the MAGs identified are new species.

Prior 16S studies suggest the most common prokaryote phylum on amphibians’ epidermis are usually Proteobacteria, Bacteriodetes, and Actinobacteria (mckenzie_2012?; jimenez_2019?; barnes_2021?; walke_2021?; martinez-ugalde_2024?; wan_2024?).

Organic pollutants, such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) which typically originate from motor vehicle exhaust and industrial activities, have also been reported at higher concentrations among historical urban parks located in larger industrialized cities with a longer history of industrial pollution (cachada_2012?).
